episodes.title: Week 9: Conversations Begin
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week nine, days sixty-three through seventy: conversations begin. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Around nine weeks, many babies are clearly social. They smile, coo, and seem to enjoy back-and-forth. Crying usually starts to ease after the six-to-eight-week peak. Many babies discover their hands and watch them with fascination.

Some babies show early signs of trying to roll. The AAP says to stop swaddling as soon as a baby shows signs of attempting to roll, and that can come earlier than parents expect.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies now follow objects through a wider arc and can look from one object to another. Color perception continues to develop. Hearing is sharp; babies often turn toward voices.

Brain exercise for this week: the conversation game. Talk to your baby, pause, and let them answer with coos. Copy their sounds. Read simple board books with bold pictures. The amount of back-and-forth talk in the first years is linked to later language skills, and you can't overdo warm, responsive talk.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often prefer singing, rhymes, and stories to electronic media. That aligns with the CDC: no screen time before age two except video calls.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

During tummy time, many babies hold their head up steadily and may push up on their forearms. On their back, they may bat at a toy dangling overhead.

Keep tummy time at thirty minutes or more a day if your baby enjoys it, as the WHO recommends for babies not yet mobile. Offer a toy just out of reach to encourage head turning and reaching.

The natural lens. A firm floor mat, minimal gear, and lots of supervised floor time are the natural-movement default. If your baby tilts the head to one side or you notice a flat spot, mention it to your pediatrician; early repositioning and tummy time help.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about seven to nine times a day. Some drop a night feed; others don't. Both are normal. Growth is judged on the growth chart, not ounces.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to five ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. For return-to-work planning, many lactation professionals use a rule of thumb of about one to one and a quarter ounces per hour of separation. That's practical guidance, not a requirement. Pump about as often as the baby feeds.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, roughly two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. If daycare bottles are coming, try a few bottle feeds from another caregiver ahead of time. Paced feeding helps a breastfed baby accept the bottle without overfeeding.

The natural lens on formula. Many families in the natural and Make America Healthy Again space prefer organic formula, formulas made with whole-milk fat, or those without corn syrup solids. The FDA's Operation Stork Speed is reviewing formula nutrients and carbohydrate sources, and its latest contaminant testing found most samples low or non-detectable. All legal U.S. formula meets FDA nutrient standards. Don't make homemade formula; the FDA warns that it can cause serious harm.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize real food and protein at each meal. If you eat low-carb, keto, or carnivore, know that there's little research on how those diets affect breast milk, and that very low-carb diets during breastfeeding have been linked to rare lactation ketoacidosis in case reports, especially with fasting or intense exercise. Our reasoning: keep some carbohydrate, eat enough, and don't fast while exclusively breastfeeding.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies have a longer first stretch of sleep. Total sleep is often around fourteen to sixteen hours. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months. Stop swaddling once there are signs of rolling.

The natural lens. Harrison's 2004 study tracked babies at nine weeks too. Better night sleepers had more early-afternoon light. Our reasoning: a daily walk in the shade after lunch is a low-risk habit worth trying.

The bed-sharing debate. Some natural-parenting families bed-share. Anthropologist James McKenna of the University of Notre Dame argues that for sober, nonsmoking, breastfeeding mothers, what he calls breastsleeping is a normal human pattern. The AAP disagrees and recommends against bed-sharing, because the risk of sleep-related death is higher. Both sides agree on the most dangerous situations: sleeping with a baby on a sofa or armchair, after alcohol or sedating medicines, with smoking, with a preterm or very young baby, or in soft bedding. The safest place for your baby to sleep is a separate, flat, bare crib or bassinet in your room. If you might fall asleep while feeding, do it in your bed, not a sofa, with pillows and blankets away from the baby, and move baby back to the crib when you wake.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

By four months, the CDC lists laughing or chuckling, cooing back, holding the head steady when held, holding a toy, swinging at toys, and pushing up onto the elbows. Teething most often starts around six months; drooling can start earlier and doesn't always mean teeth are coming. Solids start around six months with readiness signs. Sitting alone falls between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, talk with your baby, and leave space for answers.

Second, stop swaddling at the first sign of rolling.

Third, keep up daily floor time.

Fourth, plan daycare bottles with paced feeding and a realistic per-hour estimate.

Fifth, if you're eating low-carb, eat enough and keep some carbs.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too if your baby doesn't respond to sounds, doesn't watch faces, can't hold the head up at all during tummy time, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report, the CDC, the WHO, the FDA, and the named study: Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week ten.

episodes.title: Week 10: Reaching Out
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week ten, days seventy through seventy-seven: reaching out. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Around ten weeks, many babies start reaching toward the world. They may swipe or bat at a dangling toy, and their hands open more often. Smiles come easily, and cooing may sound more like conversation. Crying, for most families, is easing from its peak.

This is also a common time for a parent to go back to work, so routines are shifting. Babies often adapt better than parents expect, especially when caregivers are responsive and feeding plans are clear.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Vision is improving quickly. Babies can follow a toy from side to side and are starting to coordinate eyes and hands. Color vision is developing; bright, saturated colors attract attention.

Brain exercise for this week: reach and name. Hold a bright toy within reach, let your baby swipe, and name what happened: you touched the ball. Then let them rest. Read a short book every day, pointing at pictures. The CDC suggests talking, reading, and singing as everyday brain builders, with no screens before age two except video calls.

The natural lens. Montessori families often use a simple hanging toy, like a ring or bell on a ribbon, over a floor mat at this stage, so babies can practice batting. Evidence for the specific toy is thin; the reasoning is that babies need chances to practice reaching, and a simple setup gives them that. Always supervise, and keep cords out of reach.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies hold their head up well during tummy time and push up on their forearms. Some begin rocking or rolling slightly to the side. On their back, they kick strongly and may bring their hands together.

Keep tummy time going, thirty minutes or more a day spread out, as the WHO recommends for babies not yet mobile. Try side-lying play with a rolled towel behind the back to encourage reaching across.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates encourage barefoot floor play and minimal time in containers like car seats outside the car, bouncers, and swings. Mainstream advice agrees that container time should be limited.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about six to nine times a day, and feeds may be quick. Babies get easily distracted during feeds now; a quiet, dim room can help. Intake in exclusively breastfed babies stays fairly stable from one to six months.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to six ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. If daycare reports your baby is taking much more than you pump, ask caregivers to use paced feeding, a slow-flow nipple, and to stop at fullness cues. The rule of thumb of about one to one and a quarter ounces per hour of separation is a practical starting point, not a requirement.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, roughly two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually capped around thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. With work and daycare, many families shift to mixed feeding. Keep breastfeeding when together, and pump during separation to protect supply. Count bottles as measured and breast feeds as feeds.

The parent's plate, natural lens. Low-carb and carnivore physicians like Dr. Ken Berry argue for cutting refined sugar and highly processed foods, and many low-carb voices also argue against industrial seed oils. The new 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines also push hard against highly processed foods and added sugars, so here mainstream and natural advice overlap. The seed-oil question itself is debated, and evidence is mixed; we label that as an open question. For a nursing parent, the practical takeaway is the same: build meals around protein, real fats, vegetables, and enough total food, and don't fast.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies have one longer sleep stretch at night, and some are starting to settle into a few predictable naps. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: keep wake-up time roughly consistent, get daylight after lunch, and keep the hour before bed dim and calm. Harrison's 2004 study, which followed babies to twelve weeks, linked more early-afternoon light to better night sleep. It's correlation, but it's low risk.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

By four months, the CDC lists chuckling, turning toward your voice, holding the head steady when held, holding a toy, swinging at toys, bringing hands to the mouth, and pushing up onto elbows on the tummy. Rolling tummy to back is on the six-month list. Teething most often starts around six months, solids around six months with readiness signs, sitting alone between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, give your baby chances to reach: simple toys, close by, supervised.

Second, keep floor time and tummy time a daily habit.

Third, make feeding plans clear for caregivers, including paced bottle feeding.

Fourth, build your own meals around real food, protein, and enough of it.

Fifth, keep a consistent wake time and daylight in the afternoon.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, a baby who doesn't follow moving things with the eyes or doesn't respond to sounds, or one who seems very floppy or very stiff. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages, the CDC, the WHO, the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines, and the named studies: Rios-Leyvraz and Yao 2023 and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week eleven.

episodes.title: Week 11: Strong Arms, Round Heads
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week eleven, days seventy-seven through eighty-four: strong arms, round heads. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Around eleven weeks, many babies are pushing up during tummy time, holding their heads more steadily, and making a wider range of sounds. Some may let out their first laugh soon; the CDC's four-month checklist includes chuckling.

Drooling often increases around now. That usually reflects developing salivary glands and mouthing, not necessarily teething. First teeth most often appear around six months.

This is also a good week to look at your baby's head shape. Flat spots, called positional plagiocephaly, can develop when babies spend a lot of time lying in the same position. Tummy time and repositioning help.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies now look at faces and objects for longer, follow movement smoothly, and may recognize familiar people from across the room. They respond to tone of voice.

Brain exercise for this week: copy and stretch. Copy your baby's sound, then add a new one. They coo ah, you say ah-boo. Play simple peekaboo with a cloth. Read and sing daily.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often emphasize time outdoors, in the shade, with natural sounds and changing light, as sensory input. Our reasoning: varied real-world input, with a caring adult narrating, is what babies are built to learn from.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies push up on their forearms and hold their head and chest up for a while. Some start to roll partway onto a side. On their back, they bring hands together and to the mouth.

Head-shape check. Look down at your baby's head from above. If one side looks flatter, or the head always turns the same way, alternate the direction your baby faces in the crib, alternate which arm you hold them in, and increase supervised tummy time. Mention it at the next visit; most mild flat spots improve with repositioning.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates frame flat spots as a sign of too much container time: car seats used outside the car, swings, bouncers, and loungers. The AAP's guidance is similar. Babies should always sleep on their back, but awake time should include plenty of tummy time and fewer containers.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about six to eight times a day. Distractibility is common; feed in a quiet space if needed. Some babies start sleeping a longer night stretch and feed more during the day.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to six ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. Babies don't need bigger bottles every week, because intake in breastfed babies is fairly stable from one to six months.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, about two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces. Formula volume tends to rise with weight.

Mixed feeding. Keep a balance that protects supply if you want to keep breastfeeding: nurse when together, pump when apart.

The natural lens on gut health. Integrative pediatrician Dr. Elisa Song emphasizes protecting the infant gut microbiome, through breast milk when possible, avoiding unnecessary antibiotics and acid-suppressing medicines, and later, a diverse diet. Mainstream medicine agrees that antibiotics should be used only when needed and that acid suppression isn't recommended for uncomplicated spit-up. Breast milk contains prebiotic sugars called human milk oligosaccharides that feed beneficial bacteria; that part is well established.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize real food. Many breastfeeding parents continue a prenatal vitamin. Lily Nichols emphasizes choline from eggs, iodine, vitamin D, and omega-3s from low-mercury fish. If you're low-carb, eat enough and don't fast.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies sleep about fourteen to sixteen hours in total, with a longer night stretch. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning on rhythm: light in the morning and early afternoon, dim lights in the evening, and a short, repeatable bedtime routine: feed, bath or wipe-down, song, crib. Harrison's 2004 study linked early-afternoon light to better night sleep at six to twelve weeks.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

By four months, the CDC lists chuckling, holding the head steady without support when held, holding a toy, swinging at toys, bringing hands to the mouth, pushing up onto the elbows on the tummy, and opening the mouth when hungry at the sight of breast or bottle. By six months: rolling tummy to back, reaching for toys, and laughing. Teething usually starts around six months, solids around six months with readiness signs, sitting alone between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, check your baby's head shape and vary positions.

Second, keep tummy time generous and container time short.

Third, play copy-and-stretch sound games.

Fourth, protect the gut: breast milk if possible, and avoid unnecessary medicines.

Fifth, keep a simple bedtime routine.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for a head shape that's worsening, a head that always tilts or turns one way, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, or a baby who doesn't respond to sounds or faces. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report, the CDC, and the named studies: Rios-Leyvraz and Yao 2023 and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week twelve.

episodes.title: Week 12: End of the Fourth Trimester
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week twelve, days eighty-four through ninety-one: the end of the fourth trimester. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Three months is often called the end of the fourth trimester. Many babies are now more predictable, more social, and less fussy. Crying has usually eased from its peak. Many babies hold their heads more steadily, laugh or chuckle, and bring their hands to their mouths.

This week also opens the door to the monthly episodes in Little Steps. From here on, each episode covers a month, with week-by-week expectations inside.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies follow faces and objects smoothly, look from one thing to another, and are starting to see color well; color vision is fairly good by about four to five months. Depth perception develops a bit later, over the next few months.

Brain exercise for this week: give your baby a voice. Narrate what you think they're feeling: you're looking at the window, you hear the dog. Pause after questions. Read every day. Hold a rattle to one side and let your baby find the sound.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often keep toys simple: a rattle, a soft ball, a wooden ring, and a mirror. The reasoning is that fewer, simpler toys invite more exploration, and it costs less. Evidence for one toy over another is thin.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies push up on their forearms during tummy time, hold their head steady when held upright, and may swing at toys. Some begin rolling from tummy to back; the CDC lists that on its six-month checklist, so earlier is a bonus, not a requirement.

Once rolling begins, never leave your baby on a bed, couch, or changing table, even for a second.

The natural lens. Floor time on a firm mat remains the natural-movement priority. Mainstream advice agrees: plenty of supervised floor time and limited container time.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about six to eight times a day. The 2023 Rios-Leyvraz and Yao review found an average of about seven hundred thirty milliliters a day at three months in healthy, exclusively breastfed babies, but individual babies vary widely and the review mixes measurement methods. Your baby's growth curve is the real measure.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to six ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. Because intake is fairly stable from one to six months, pumped-milk needs usually don't climb much from here.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, often around twenty-four to thirty-two ounces a day, using the AAP guide of about two and a half ounces per pound per day and a cap of about thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles, count breast feeds, and don't add guessed ounces.

Looking ahead to iron. The AAP recommends that exclusively breastfed babies start an iron supplement of one milligram per kilogram per day at four months, until iron-rich foods are part of the diet. Formula is fortified with iron. The natural lens: many families in this space would rather meet iron needs with food, and meat and egg yolk are iron-rich first foods. But solids aren't recommended until around six months, so the four-to-six-month gap is a real question to discuss with your pediatrician.

Solids, a preview. The AAP, CDC, and WHO recommend starting solids around six months, not before four months, when babies show readiness signs: sitting with support, good head control, interest in food, and the ability to move food to the back of the mouth instead of pushing it out. Not yet. No cereal in bottles.

The parent's plate. Keep eating real food. If you're returning to low-carb or keto, ease in, keep calories adequate, and avoid fasting while exclusively breastfeeding.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies sleep about fourteen to sixteen hours in total. Some begin sleeping longer stretches at night; others don't yet, and that's normal. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Harrison's 2004 study found babies who slept well at six weeks tended to sleep well at twelve, and that better sleepers had more early-afternoon light. Our reasoning: keep the light rhythm going. A sleep shift often happens around four months, so a steady routine now helps.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Coming in month three and four: laughing, cooing back, holding a toy, swinging at toys, bringing hands to the mouth, and pushing up on the elbows. By six months: rolling tummy to back, reaching, and blowing raspberries. Teething most often starts around six months, with a wide range. Sitting alone falls between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, enjoy a more social, predictable baby.

Second, never leave your baby on a raised surface.

Third, ask your pediatrician about iron at four months if your baby is exclusively breastfed.

Fourth, learn the readiness signs for solids, but wait for them.

Fifth, keep the light-and-dark rhythm steady.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, or a baby who doesn't follow faces, doesn't respond to sounds, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

episodes.title: Month 3
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month three: Build a flexible rhythm. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Picture a day with a little more predictability, but plenty of surprises. Rather than setting a rigid timetable, try repeating a few gentle cues: conversation during a diaper change, a short play session when alert, and quieter surroundings before sleep. Keep feeding responsive to hunger and fullness.

Your baby's next CDC milestone checkpoint is four months. You may start watching for interest in hands, cooing, or attempts to keep your attention. These are possibilities to notice, not claims about what your baby is doing already. Respond to sounds, offer a safe easy-to-hold toy, and give supervised floor time.

Rolling preparation matters now. Stop swaddling at any sign of trying to roll, and always start sleep on the back. Breast milk or formula remains the food at this stage; being curious about your dinner does not by itself mean readiness for solids. Today's useful goal is one dependable calming routine and one enjoyable face-to-face moment. If development or feeding worries you, bring it up rather than waiting for an app to tell you everything is fine.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.title: Month 4
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month four: Hands become an adventure. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Watch those hands. The CDC's four-month checklist includes looking at hands with interest, bringing them to the mouth, and holding a toy placed in the hand. Offer a clean, age-appropriate toy that is not sharp, hot, or small enough to choke on. Stay involved and let the baby explore at their own pace.

Talk back when your baby makes sounds. Read a picture book by naming what you see, even if you only make it through one page. During supervised tummy time, give space to push up and look around. If a milestone is missing or you have concerns, discuss it with the clinician; the checklist is a conversation starter, not a diagnosis.

This is also a good time to plan for solids, not rush them. General guidance is around six months when the baby is developmentally ready, and not before four months. Until then, breast milk or formula continues. Keep the sleep space empty, and stop swaddling with any rolling attempts. Today's job is one safe toy and a few minutes of shared exploration.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.title: Month 5
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month five: Get ready, without rushing. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The family table may suddenly look fascinating. Watching you eat is a lovely social moment, but interest alone is not the green light for solids. Around six months, look for a collection of readiness signs: steady head and neck control, sitting with support or alone, opening the mouth for food, and swallowing rather than pushing everything back out.

Use this month to talk with your clinician about first foods and choking prevention. If your baby has severe eczema or an egg allergy, ask specifically about safely introducing peanut-containing foods. There is no need to buy an elaborate feeding system to have this conversation.

For now, offer responsive milk feeds and supervised floor play. The next CDC checkpoint, at six months, includes reaching for a wanted toy, laughing, and taking turns making sounds. You can support those opportunities without making them homework. Put a safe toy nearby, respond to a squeal, and pause. Today's action is preparation: write down your questions about readiness and choose a calm, supervised place for future meals.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.title: Month 6
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month six: First tastes, safely. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Imagine a small spoonful, a puzzled expression, and most of it landing on the bib. Starting solids is practice, not a race to replace milk. Around six months, when readiness signs are present, begin developmentally suitable foods while continuing breast milk or formula as the main source of nutrition.

Start with a small amount of a single-ingredient food. The CDC advises waiting three to five days between new foods initially so problems are easier to spot. Offer variety over time, including fortified infant cereal and other foods from different groups. Keep textures soft and appropriate, and stay right beside your baby for eating.

Potential allergens belong in the introduction plan, not on an automatic delay list. Ask first about peanut introduction if there is severe eczema or egg allergy. Whole nuts and spoonfuls of thick nut butter are not safe serving forms. No honey before twelve months, and no cow's milk as the main drink before then. Today's goal is a safe, calm first experience, not a clean bowl.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.title: Month 7
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month seven: Let the menu grow. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The menu can begin to feel more like a tiny version of family food. By seven or eight months, many babies can explore foods from several food groups, prepared safely for their skills. Think soft vegetables, fruit, proteins, and a variety of fortified cereals, not one food expected to do every job.

Texture changes should follow ability, with you watching closely. Mash or puree food as needed, cook hard foods until soft, and remove bones, pits, and other hazards. Never hand over a whole grape or a round slice of sausage. Eating happens seated and supervised, not while wandering or riding around.

Watch for fullness: closing the mouth or turning away is information, not a challenge to overcome. Continue breast milk or formula, and let the clinician guide you if intake or growth is concerning. Your small task today is to offer one safe texture or flavor without pressure. A funny face does not prove a permanent dislike. You can offer the food again another day while keeping the experience calm.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.title: Month 8
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month eight: A safe place to explore. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Get down to floor level for a moment and look around. What can little hands reach? As movement changes, a room that was safe last month may need another review. Move sharp and breakable things, lock away medicines and cleaning products, and remove small objects from the play area.

Offer a safe toy a little out of reach and stay close while the baby works out how to approach it. There is no need to force crawling or compare one movement style with another. The nine-month CDC checklist ahead includes sitting without support, getting into sitting, and transferring things between hands. Ask about any concerns rather than turning one skill into the whole story.

Play can be delightfully ordinary: pass a toy back and forth, name a picture, or repeat a sound. Keep meals seated and supervised, with food prepared for the baby's current skills. Today's action is a floor-level safety sweep, then a few minutes of play together. Safe space plus your attention is more valuable than a complicated activity.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.title: Month 9
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month nine: The disappearing spoon game. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The spoon drops. You pick it up. It drops again. This may feel repetitive, but looking for dropped objects is one of the skills on the CDC's nine-month checklist. A simple back-and-forth game gives you a way to share the discovery without needing a new toy.

At this checkpoint, notice sitting without support, varied babbling, looking when called by name, and moving objects between hands. These checklists describe what most babies can do by an age, and they are not diagnostic tests. Share concerns or lost skills with your clinician promptly, and ask about developmental screening.

Some babies also react more strongly when a caregiver leaves. Try a short, cheerful goodbye rather than sneaking away, and greet them warmly when you return. Keep familiar routines and allow time to get used to another caregiver. Today's practical plan is one little turn-taking game and one predictable goodbye. Your baby does not need to handle every new situation happily for you to be supporting them well.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.title: Month 10
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month ten: Small hands, big experiments. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

A cup, a safe container, and a few large baby-safe toys can turn the floor into a discovery lab. Show putting a toy in and taking it out. Let your baby watch or join in, without requiring a particular result. The one-year CDC checkpoint ahead includes putting something into a container and finding a toy hidden in front of them.

Keep talking through everyday moments. Name the cup, describe the ball, and respond to sounds or gestures. A shared picture book can be a conversation about pictures rather than a full reading of the words. Real back-and-forth matters more than a learning video.

At meals, continue safe textures and close supervision. Small foods must be prepared to avoid choking; small does not automatically mean safe. Keep honey and juice off the menu before the first birthday, and continue breast milk or formula. Today's small win is one simple container game and a check that every toy is age-appropriate, intact, and too large to choke on.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.title: Month 11
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month eleven: Prepare for the next chapter. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The first birthday is coming, but independent walking is not a birthday entrance requirement. The CDC's one-year checklist includes pulling up to stand and walking while holding furniture. Offer a safe place to practice and stay close. Do not use a baby walker; safe floor exploration is a better choice.

This is a good month to plan the next checkup. Write down questions about development, meals, and the transition from formula after twelve months. The CDC says plain, unsweetened, pasteurized whole cow's milk can replace formula at that stage; discuss alternatives or individual needs with the clinician. Breastfeeding can continue if parent and child want it. There is no deadline to stop because a candle appears.

Keep food preparation safe and the sleep space appropriate. Practice a cup with help during a calm meal, and expect spills. Today's task is planning, not rushing: a question list for the clinician and a safe bit of furniture for supported practice. Your baby's pace deserves attention, not a countdown.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.title: Month 12: One Year!
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month twelve: A year of little steps. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Welcome to the first-birthday chapter. Whether you are listening ahead or arriving at this stage, take a breath. There is no single picture of a one-year-old. The CDC's reference points include waving goodbye, using a special name for a parent, pulling to stand, cruising along furniture, and picking up small bits of food between thumb and finger.

Look at the whole picture and bring questions to the clinician. If a skill has been lost or something concerns you, ask for developmental screening rather than waiting. Celebrate attempts without turning the checklist into a score.

Food and drink move into a new stage. After twelve months, many children can transition from formula to plain pasteurized whole milk, with the clinician helping tailor the plan. Breastfeeding may continue. Keep offering varied, safely prepared foods, help with a cup, and skip sugary drinks; juice is unnecessary. Use positive words and gentle redirection as curiosity grows. Today's celebration can be simple: share a book, a song, or a game together. The next chapter still starts with small, responsive moments.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.
